---
title: "Coming from jsonlite"
description: "Where zujson and jsonlite give different results for the same input, and the argument that closes each gap."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zujson)
```

This guide is for someone who knows
[jsonlite](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=jsonlite) and is moving code
to zujson, or deciding whether to. It lists every place the two give
different results at their defaults, in parsing, writing and failing, with
the argument that brings them back into agreement where there is one.

The functions correspond like this:

| jsonlite | zujson |
| --- | --- |
| `fromJSON(txt)` on a string | `json_parse(txt)` |
| `fromJSON(path)` on a file | `json_parse_file(path)` |
| `toJSON(x)` | `json_write(x)` |
| `toJSON(x, auto_unbox = TRUE)` | `json_write(x)`, which unboxes by default |
| `validate(txt)` | `json_validate(txt)` |
| `stream_in()`, `stream_out()` | `json_parse_ndjson()`, `json_write_ndjson()`, on a whole body |

jsonlite is much broader. Everything below is the price of a mapping small
enough to hold in your head, and all of it is pinned in the package's own
tests, which use jsonlite as an oracle over JSON text, so a divergence that
stops being deliberate fails the suite.

Every cell in the tables below is computed by running both packages when
this page is built.


```{r include = FALSE}
library(jsonlite)

# One compact line per R value. Data frames and matrices are rebuilt as the
# call that would make them, which is shorter than deparsing the attributes
# and still says exactly what came back.
fmt <- function(x) {
  if (is.data.frame(x)) {
    cols <- vapply(x, function(col) paste(deparse(col), collapse = ""), "")
    return(sprintf("data.frame(%s)",
                   paste(names(x), cols, sep = " = ", collapse = ", ")))
  }
  if (is.matrix(x)) {
    return(sprintf("matrix(%s, nrow = %d)",
                   paste(deparse(as.vector(x)), collapse = ""), nrow(x)))
  }
  paste(deparse(x, width.cutoff = 500), collapse = " ")
}
code <- function(x) paste0("`", x, "`")

# Evaluating the same expression that gets printed as the label is what keeps
# the two columns honest: there is no second copy to fall out of step.
run <- function(e, f) {
  tryCatch(f(eval(e)), zujson_error = function(c) paste0("error: ", class(c)[1]),
           error = function(c) paste0("error: ", class(c)[1]))
}
label <- function(e) paste(deparse(e), collapse = "")
```

## Parsing

Most JSON reads the same way in both: objects, nulls, scalars, escapes,
surrogate pairs and the integer boundaries all agree. Four things do not, and
three of them have an opt-in that closes the gap.

```{r echo = FALSE}
js <- c("[]", '[1, "a"]', '[{"a":1},{"b":2}]', "[[1,2],[3,4]]")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  JSON = code(js),
  zujson = code(vapply(js, function(j) fmt(json_parse(j)), "")),
  jsonlite = code(vapply(js, function(j) fmt(fromJSON(j)), "")),
  `Opt-in that agrees` = c("none needed --- see below",
                           '`simplify = "coerce"`',
                           "`data_frame = TRUE`",
                           "none; no matrix detection"),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
), row.names = FALSE)
```

The record case is explicit because turning records into a data frame
changes what a missing key means, and the matrix case because JSON carries
no dimensions to infer one from.

The empty array is the one with no opt-in and no argument about it: with no
elements to take a type from, the zero-length atomic vector is as good an
answer as the empty list, and this package prefers the one that keeps `[]` and
`[1,2]` in the same family.

## Serializing

This is where the two differ most, because `toJSON()` has a dozen arguments
shaping its output and `json_write()` has two.

```{r echo = FALSE}
es <- list(
  quote(35),
  quote(c(a = 1, b = 2)),
  quote(c(1, NA, Inf)),
  quote(pi),
  quote(NULL),
  quote(as.POSIXct("2013-06-17 22:33:44", tz = "UTC")),
  quote(matrix(1:4, 2)),
  quote(complex(real = 2, imaginary = 2)),
  quote(charToRaw("bla")),
  quote(as.POSIXlt("2013-06-17 22:33:44", tz = "UTC"))
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `R value` = code(vapply(es, label, "")),
  zujson = code(vapply(es, run, "", f = json_write)),
  `jsonlite, at its defaults` =
    code(vapply(es, run, "", f = function(x) as.character(toJSON(x)))),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
), row.names = FALSE)
```

Four of those are worth a sentence.

The unboxing defaults are **opposite**: `json_write()` unboxes a length-1
vector and `toJSON()` does not, which is the first thing to trip over when
porting code. A **named atomic vector** is an object here and an array there,
and this is the one with no argument that reconciles it --- `toJSON()` drops
vector names unless asked with `keep_vec_names`, which it also warns about.
Every **missing or non-finite** value is `null` here, where `toJSON()`'s
default makes a numeric `NA` the *string* `"NA"` while a character or logical
`NA` becomes `null`. And **doubles** are written so they read back as the same
number, rather than rounded to four digits.

The refusals at the bottom of the table are deliberate: a complex number, a
raw vector and a `POSIXlt` have no obvious JSON form, so they raise
`zujson_unsupported_type` instead of being guessed at. A data frame column that
is itself a data frame is refused for the same reason. `POSIXct` is always UTC,
which is the same instant whatever `tzone` says.

## Failing

The divergence that matters most to a client: every failure here is a typed
condition rather than a bare `simpleError`, so one handler catches the lot and
can still tell the cases apart.

```{r echo = FALSE}
cls <- function(e) paste(class(tryCatch(eval(e), error = function(c) c))[1])
deep <- paste0(strrep("[", 1500), strrep("]", 1500))
nul <- '["a\\u0000b"]'
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Input = c("`\"{bad\"`", "an escaped NUL, `\"\\u0000\"`",
            "nesting 1500 deep", "a URL or file path"),
  zujson = c(code(cls(quote(json_parse("{bad")))),
             code(cls(quote(json_parse(nul)))),
             code(cls(quote(json_parse(deep)))),
             "never read; `json_parse_file()` is explicit"),
  jsonlite = c(code(cls(quote(fromJSON("{bad")))),
               paste0("silently truncates to ", code(fromJSON(nul))),
               "C stack overflow",
               "fetched or read"),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
), row.names = FALSE)
```

The middle two are the ones to notice. An escaped NUL is valid JSON that no R
string can hold, so refusing it is the only honest answer --- returning a
silently shortened string loses data without saying so. And the depth cap turns
what would be a C stack overflow into a condition you can catch, which is what
makes the parser safe to point at a body you did not write.
